title: Comfort ye (Isaiah 40:1–11)
hookLine: speak tenderly; every valley lifted; he gathers the lambs in his arms

cards: Read Isaiah straight through and something happens at chapter forty. Chapter after chapter has been warnings, judgments and armies. Assyria is coming.
Jerusalem is in danger. The chapter just before ends with a warning that the king's treasures, and his sons, will one day be carried off to Babylon. Then you turn the page, and the voice changes.
Now it speaks to a city whose hard service is over, and to a people who need a road home. And the first word God speaks to them isn't a rebuke, or an explanation, or a lesson about what went wrong.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God." Said twice, the way you'd say it to someone crying: it's okay, it's okay. In Hebrew it's nachamu, nachamu ammi.

teach.h: SPEAK TO THE HEART OF JERUSALEM.
teach.b: Literally, speak to the heart of Jerusalem: the phrase used elsewhere in the Bible for someone wooing, or reassuring, someone they love. Tell her, God says, that her hard service is over.
Then a voice cries out: make a road through the wilderness for God.
"Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain."

Road builders filling every dip and leveling every hill, so God can come straight to his people and bring them home. People are like grass, the chapter reminds them; the grass withers, but God's word stands.

And it ends tenderly: "He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young." Not driving the flock.
Carrying the smallest, walking slowly for the mothers. Some scholars think this chapter begins a new part of the book, written later for the exiles; others hold the whole book to be Isaiah's.
Christians hear the voice in the wilderness as John the Baptist, as all four Gospels say.
And Jewish communities read this chapter on the Sabbath after Tisha B'Av, the fast that mourns the Temple: they call it the Sabbath of comfort.

how: Christians read Isaiah 40 in Advent, often alongside the story of John the Baptist, and Handel's Messiah opens with it; in Jewish practice it is the prophetic reading on Shabbat Nachamu, the Sabbath after Tisha B'Av.

o: a royal order to stop mourning at once
God's first word to his people: be comforted
a blessing said over food at a feast

games.q: what's inside the chapter — tap the pairs.

s: God's first word to the exiles is a rebuke
it's comfort, said twice: "comfort ye, comfort ye my people."
all four Gospels connect the voice in the wilderness with John the Baptist
Matthew, Mark, Luke and John all use Isaiah 40:3 for him.
the shepherd drives the whole flock at the same pace
he carries the lambs and gently leads the mothers.

games.q: you're sent to speak to exiles who lost everything, partly through their own choices. what's your first word?
o: here is what you did wrong.
be patient: it will all make sense one day.
games.why: "comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God." the first word after the long warning is tenderness, spoken to the heart.

practice: Think of someone in a hard season, worn out, far from home, grieving, or just tired of being told what they did wrong, and set down the urge to fix them or explain things.
Instead, imagine speaking to their heart, the way this chapter does: what would you say first? Keep it short and kind, say it silently twice, and if you pray, pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Comfort ye. Nachamu in Hebrew: the first word of a new section of Isaiah, spoken twice, speaking tenderly to the heart.

orig.note: Hebrew: comfort, comfort my people. the opening words of Isaiah 40.

carryVoice: Your line: comfort ye my people. Comfort first, before any lesson. Day four hundred sixty-seven, done.
